note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting with vomiting and diarrhoea since last night.
The patient has had about five bile-stained, green vomits since last night, with fewer today.
The patient has had six to seven loose stools today.
There is blood in the patient's stool.
The patient's brother had a similar illness from nursery, and the patient attends the same nursery.
The patient has had four wet nappies since this morning.
The patient is taking small amounts of breast milk and formula.
The patient is alert and playing.
The patient is not drowsy or floppy.
The patient has no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
Examination was a telephone assessment and no physical examination was performed.
The impression is probable viral gastroenteritis with reduced urine output.
The plan is a face-to-face assessment at the surgery today at 16:00.
The plan is to continue breastfeeding and give small amounts of oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) every few minutes.
Safety netting includes calling 999 if the patient becomes floppy, very sleepy, or hard to wake, or if a rash does not fade when pressed.
Safety netting includes attending A&E if the vomit goes green or if there is blood in the nappy.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician initiated contact by asking if the caller was Freya's mother.
The relative identified herself as Leanne.
The clinician identified herself as Dr Mistry calling back from the surgery.
The relative confirmed Freya was on her lap.
The clinician asked to confirm Freya's date of birth.
Freya's date of birth is the fourteenth of December, and she is ten months old.
Freya started being sick last night and had diarrhoea this morning.
Freya has been sick about five times since last night, with fewer today.
The vomit is milky, not green.
The relative reported six or seven runny dirty nappies today.
There is no blood in Freya's nappies, but her brother had blood in his last week when he had the same illness.
Freya's brother had a similar illness at nursery, and Freya attends the same nursery.
The relative initially thought there were about four wet nappies, but corrected this to only two wet ones since this morning, with the others being dirty.
There are two wet nappies since this morning, and the current time is about two o'clock.
Freya is having little bits of milk and is breastfed and has a bit of formula.
Freya's temperature this morning was 37.4 °C.
Freya is grumpy but is watching the telly and playing with her blocks.
Freya is not very sleepy or floppy or hard to wake.
There is no rash.
The patient has no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
The clinician suggested the condition is likely probable viral gastroenteritis with reduced urine output.
The clinician expressed concern about the low number of wet nappies (two) and requested a face-to-face assessment at four o'clock.
The clinician advised continuing to breastfeed and giving small amounts of oral rehydration solution (like Dioralyte) a teaspoon every few minutes.
The clinician advised calling 999 if the patient becomes floppy, very sleepy, or hard to wake, or gets a rash that doesn't fade when pressed.
The clinician advised taking the patient to A&E if the vomit goes green or if there is blood in the nappy.
